analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate from 34% to 15% and adjusts asset values upward for inflation before taxing gains.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 1990 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no further action; it died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the tax rate on profits from selling stocks and other long-held assets from 34% to 15%, with an even lower 7.5% rate for low- and middle-income filers. It would also have adjusted the original purchase price of corporate stock and business property upward for inflation before calculating taxable gains, so less of the profit counts as taxable. Wealthy households and large investors, who hold most of these assets, would have seen the biggest dollar benefit.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations that own stocks and business property and sell at a profit. Because capital gains flow overwhelmingly to higher-income households, the largest dollar savings would go to the wealthiest taxpayers and to corporations selling appreciated assets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and corporations selling appreciated assets

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the maximum tax rate on long-term capital gains for both individuals and corporations from 34% to 15%, and to 7.5% for low- and middle-income taxpayers [S2][S3].

Adjusts the basis of corporate stock and business property held more than a year upward for inflation before computing gain, so a portion of the profit that is simply inflation is no longer taxed [S2][S3].
Reduces the minimum-tax rate applied to capital gains and indexes the annual limit on capital losses for individuals ($3,000/$1,500) to inflation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, meaning either taxpayers generally through higher deficits or through other taxes replacing the lost revenue. Gains from asset sales are concentrated among higher-income households, so the lost revenue would come while the tax system shifted further toward taxing ordinary wage income relative to investment income.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal Treasury and wage earners

drawbacks.text: Cutting the capital gains rate from 34% to 15% and indexing basis for inflation would sharply reduce federal revenue, since capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households and corporations [S2][S3].

The bill excludes a large share of assets from indexing (options, preferred stock, S corporation stock, foreign stock in most cases, net lease property) [S3], creating complexity and uneven treatment that many tax analysts criticized in indexing proposals of this era.

Lower rates on investment gains relative to wages widen the gap between how work and wealth are taxed, which supporters of the bill's opponents generally acknowledged would primarily benefit the top of the income distribution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's 7.5% rate for low- and middle-income taxpayers and inflation protection against being taxed on gains that are only price-level changes are real ideas with some fairness logic. But the design's dominant effect is a large rate cut from 34% to 15% on all long-term gains, and the dollar value of that cut rises with the size of the gain, so the benefits would flow mainly to the households and corporations holding the most appreciated assets. The revenue cost would be borne broadly, including by people who hold few or no appreciated assets.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 1990 and the committee never acted on it; the Congress ended in January 1991 and the bill died without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mickey Edwards introduced the bill on July 25, 1990, with four Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1][S5].
No further action was taken in the committee; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill received no markup, floor vote, or Senate counterpart action in the record [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No beneficiary emerged because the bill never advanced; the existing tax treatment of capital gains continued unchanged, and the federal Treasury did not lose the revenue a rate cut from 34% to 15% would have cost.

for.name: Mickey Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full text in the House.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled markup or floor action; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to markup or to the House floor during the 1990 session.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were House Republicans (the sponsor and four cosponsors) [S4], and the committee that declined to act was controlled by House Democrats, who held 257 of 435 seats; no Democrats are recorded in support.

industries.industry: Investors in corporate stock and business property
industries.note: The bill cuts their tax rate on asset sales from 34% to 15% and shields inflation from tax. Because capital gains concentrate among high-income households and corporations, the benefit flows to the top while the revenue cost falls on the broader tax base.

industries.industry: Mutual funds, REITs, and common trust funds
industries.note: The indexing rules extend to stock held through regulated investment companies, real estate investment trusts, and common trust funds, passing inflation adjustments through to fund investors [S3]. This would raise after-tax returns for fund shareholders, a group skewed toward wealthier households.

Business tangible property and partnership interests qualify for inflation indexing, with adjustments passed through to partners [S3]. Long-term holders of commercial property selling at nominal gains would pay tax on a smaller gain.
